after: How block timing informs a forecast
note: Adds the missing mechanism before evaluation: observed pace informs projected duration, then projected difficulty. before: A difficulty forecast can use current difficulty, the block where the next adjustment occurs and the time elapsed between observed Bitcoin blocks. The method needs to identify those blocks and when the inputs were recorded.

Blocks do not arrive at regular intervals. Extending the pace so far into the rest of the adjustment period requires an assumption about future block timing. It does not measure a future network value. The estimated calendar date can change too.
after: Bitcoin adjusts difficulty every 2,016 blocks to target about ten minutes per block. Within its protocol limits, the adjustment scales current difficulty by the target duration divided by the measured duration. Faster blocks point towards a higher next difficulty; slower blocks point towards a lower one.

A simple forecast estimates the full period’s duration by extending the block pace observed so far. It uses that estimate in the adjustment rule to project difficulty. This needs current difficulty, the target block and the observed blocks’ heights and timestamps.

Blocks arrive irregularly, so the pace can change as more arrive. Extending the observed pace assumes it will continue through the remaining blocks. The projected difficulty and calendar date can therefore change; neither is a measured future value.

before: Blocks arrive irregularly, so estimates over short and long windows can differ. Comparing two charts also requires matching timestamps and difficulty inputs. A change on a chart alone does not establish that mining capacity has changed.
after: Blocks arrive irregularly. Suppose two estimates use different windows ending at the same time. A run of faster blocks has more influence on the shorter window. The longer window includes more earlier blocks, so the same run has less influence.

The short-window estimate can therefore rise while the longer-window estimate changes little. That difference alone does not establish that more mining machines have joined the network. The longer window smooths recent variation, but is less responsive to a recent change.

Different timestamps or difficulty inputs can also account for a gap between charts. A 144-block window is not always 24 hours, because those blocks can arrive faster or slower. Matching the end time and units helps separate a difference in the calculation from a difference in the period being observed.

The method needs to explain what uncertainty the band includes. For example, a band describing variation from irregular block timing does not establish that the difficulty input or observation time is correct. Its width alone does not show that the estimate is accurate.
This article does not report measured band widths or identify a recent network movement as noise.
